title: With World Cup and Olympic berths at stake, revamped Canadian women's team could begin new chapter
summary: With a win over Panama at the CONCACAF W championships this Saturday, the Canadian women’s national team can clinch a berth to the 2027 World Cup and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

image.caption: Canada's Kaylee Hunter, left, shown in action during a match against Denmark on Oct. 9, is part of the Canadian women's national team that will be looking for a crucial win over Panama this weekend at the CONCACAF W Championship. (The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Soccer·Preview
With a win over Panama at the CONCACAF W championships this Saturday, the Canadian women’s national team can clinch a berth to the 2027 World Cup and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Canadians face Panama at the CONCACAF W championships on Saturday in Houston
The 2026 FIFA Men’s World Cup proved to the world that Canada is a soccer nation.
This Saturday, at Texas Health Mansfield Stadium, the Canadian women’s national team can amplify that reputation.
With a win over Panama at the CONCACAF W championships, the women’s side has a chance to clinch a berth to the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

That entails decisively conquering an opponent they beat 1-0 in 2022 — which came with an allegation of “spying” levied against them. The complaint never reached the disciplinary committee because there was no evidence.

Canada has won the continental tournament twice before but is looking to secure qualification to next year's World Cup hosted by Brazil. The Canadians are placed ninth by FIFA rankings, and Panama is 54th.

While there is always a pause to think about the worst-case scenario, the Canadian women's team goes into this tournament very well prepared. Their recent series against Denmark left with one win (in penalty shots) and one loss but a lot of lessons learned. After a loss 4-3 against Denmark on Thanksgiving Monday at BMO Field in Toronto, head coach Casey Stoney told the media that it was necessary to “keep context and not panic.”

items: Canada's women's soccer team can kill two birds with one stone

blocks.text: Context is essential for this tournament and Stoney understands what is at stake.

It is not impossible for Canada to qualify for the World Cup nor the Olympics if they don’t win against Panama, but the path is far more difficult. A journey that Stoney and the team would likely want to avoid.

Stoney, a legend on England’s national women’s team with 130 caps, learned some hard lessons, on losing in transition and the need to kill the game quickly. Something they will need to do with Panama.
Canada’s storied backline will not have Vanessa Gilles, one of its strongest players, who is unavailable due to injury.

But this team will boast a fresh and clinical group of attackers — something missing from previous iterations of this team after the retirement of the world's top international goal scorer and Canada’s skipper, Christine Sinclair, in 2023.
Kaylee Hunter, the 18-year old phenom from Calgary, will be back with a team of seasoned players including Jessie Fleming, 2026 NWSL Defender of the Year Janine Sonis, and Kadeisha Buchanan.

items: Meet budding Canadian soccer star Olivia Smith: ‘The potential to be one of the best in the world’

blocks.text: Hunter just renewed her contract with AFC Toronto in the Northern Super League (NSL). She made a name for herself on the international stage when she scored a hat trick against France at the U20 Women’s World Cup in Poland during the September window.

Hunter is the top youth player in the country and has chosen to stay in Canada and compete at the highest level. This is a particularly poignant move after Hunter was part of the AFC Toronto club that won the Diana B. Matheson Cup after beating the Montreal Roses in the NSL Final.

The Canadian women's national side features five players from Canada’s domestic league, including fellow attacker Delaney Baie Pridham — who scored her first international goal in the Toronto match against Denmark.

The attacking line is punctuated by Olivia Smith of Arsenal FC, and also midfielder Simi Awujo of Manchester United FC, both of whom are enjoying success in goal scoring and in wins in the Women’s Super League (WSL).
Marie-Yasmine (Mimi) Alidou plays midfield for the Montreal Roses and will support attackers as club rivalries are put aside for the country. All need to be finding the back of the net.

items: Buchanan, Smith highlight Canadian women's roster for World Cup, Olympic qualifier

blocks.text: Instead of turning a new leaf of attacking prowess, Canada should be thinking about planting deep roots, says Amy Walsh, soccer commentator and former captain of the national team.
Walsh, a Canada Soccer Hall of Fame inductee, says that a new approach doesn't have to be drastic, but this team has to find its form.

“It has to reaffirm its identity as one of the toughest teams to play against, that lock down defensively,” Walsh said. “So you put [clinical finishers and defensive strength] together, and I think it allows this foundational style of play, this philosophy, to take shape and put down roots.”
The women's national team has not beaten a top 15-ranked team in Stoney’s tenure that began in January 2025.
A shift away from former mainstays

With a change in roster announcements and the exclusion of players who were once considered mainstays, the shift is important considering what is at stake. Nichelle Prince (119 caps with the senior team) was named as a practice player.
“Those conversations are not easy to have,” Stoney admitted on a media call following the squad announcement. Stoney said that when she spoke with Prince, she said it was Prince’s choice.
Another player to not make the roster was Adriana Leon (132 caps).

Stoney said it was simply because Leon had not featured regularly at her club San Diego FC. She says that getting “consistent minutes” is a priority in selection. Game experience offers an opportunity to stay sharp for an intense campaign with the national team, preparedness in fitness, and practiced in game IQ.

This is the first match with consequences that the Canadian women's national program has played since 2024. They have had international friendlies but nothing this consequential.

Stoney says that they have spent a lot of time preparing and want to qualify for both Brazil and Los Angeles, but also challenge the United States for the CONCACAF title. A win against the reigning CONCACAF W champions would boost their confidence moving towards a World Cup year.
Walsh agreed that the team is up for the challenge.

“I think they come into this understanding what's on the line, and I think they're very well prepared, and they understand the task in front of them, but they also understand how to get success playing ‘Stoney Ball.’”
Stoney Ball considers that structural pieces can be tweaked but also how a “team-first mentality” is essential.
The team has faced ups and downs but its culture and identity are one that has always carried a firm belief in the collective.
With this next chapter for Canada, the game plan must be to demonstrate how lethal, decisive and unflappable it can be.
Stoney leads the charge with seasoned vets and young blood to write a new chapter for Canada women’s soccer.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Shireen Ahmed is a multi-platform sports journalist, a TEDx speaker, mentor, and an award-winning sports activist who focuses on the intersections of racism and misogyny in sports. She is an industry expert on Muslim women in sports, and her academic research and contributions have been widely published. She is co-creator and co-host of the “Burn It All Down” feminist sports podcast team. In addition to being a seasoned investigative reporter, her commentary is featured by media outlets in Canada, the USA, Europe and Australia. She holds an MA in Media Production from Toronto Metropolitan University where she now teaches Sports Journalism and Sports Media.
